To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

people infer that foods that are organic are lower in calories than foods that are conventional (Study 1), and that people believe that a person who has just eaten a conventional rather than organic dessert should exercise more to compensate (Study 2).
people perceive organic food to be healthier, and they are less likely to recommend exercise when they believe that the person is consuming organic food.
people infer that organic products are healthier, and this inference can bias everyday judgments about dieting and exercise.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of food labels on health-related judgments.
the influence of food labels on health-related judgments and behavior.
the influence of organic claims on calorie judgments and exercise behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the organic food is healthy and the organic food is not healthy.
the organic/natural label is a source of information that is capable of influencing judgments about diet and health.
organic food is not healthier than non-organic food, and the evidence that it is healthier is inconclusive and contradictory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
people infer that organic foods are healthier than their conventional counterparts and that these beliefs can have real-world consequences for health-related behaviors.
people infer that organic foods are healthy and thus lower in calories.
people infer that organic foods are lower in calories than non-organic foods, and that this inference is more pronounced when people are high in pro-environmental attitudes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people’s inferences about the nutritional content of foods are not only influenced by their actual nutritional content but also by their beliefs about how the foods were produced.
people’s inferences from the organic label may be less about health benefits than they are about the environment.
the organic label can influence people’s health decisions, even in the absence of any explicit claims about health.
